# 2 Maccabees Chapter 7 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 7 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_007_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 7 is the theological and literary pinnacle of 2 Maccabees. The martyrdom of the mother and seven sons is the earliest extended literary treatment of bodily resurrection as the explicit motivation for martyrdom. It contains three of the most theologically significant statements in the deuterocanon: the second son's proclamation of resurrection (v. 9), the mother's confession of creation ex nihilo (v. 28), and the seventh son's intercessory self-offering for the nation (vv. 37–38). All three agents recognize the chapter's gravity. PNEUMA produces its most powerful translation; EMET preserves the formal weight; LOGOS achieves the best balance of accuracy and force. This SOPHIA consensus represents a close engagement with the Greek throughout.

---

**1** It happened also that seven brothers were arrested together with their mother, and the king tried to compel them by means of whips and scourges to eat unlawful pork.

**2** One of them, speaking for the rest, said: "What do you intend to ask of us and find out? We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers."

**3** The king was enraged and gave orders for pans and caldrons to be heated.

**4** These were heated at once. He commanded the tongue of the spokesman to be cut out, his scalp to be torn off, and his hands and feet to be cut off, while the rest of the brothers and the mother watched.

**5** When the man was utterly incapacitated, the king ordered him brought to the fire still breathing and fried in the pan. As the smoke from the pan spread far and wide, the brothers and their mother encouraged one another to die nobly, saying:

**6** "The LORD God is watching, and he truly has compassion on us, as Moses declared in his song that bears witness against the people to their face: 'And he will have compassion on his servants.'"

**7** When the first had died in this way, they brought forward the second for their sport. After tearing off the skin of his head with the hair, they asked him: "Will you eat rather than have your body punished limb by limb?"

**8** He answered in the language of his ancestors: "Never." And so he in turn underwent the next stages of torture,

**9** and at his last breath he said: "You accursed wretch — you are dismissing us from this present life, but the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life, because we have died for his laws."

**10** After him, the third was subjected to their cruelty. When commanded, he put out his tongue promptly and stretched out his hands courageously,

**11** and said nobly: "I received these from Heaven, and for the sake of his laws I hold them cheap, and from him I hope to receive them back again."

**12** The king himself and those with him were struck with astonishment at the spirit of the young man, for he regarded his sufferings as nothing.

**13** When he too had died, they tortured the fourth in the same way.

**14** When he was near death, he said: "It is better to die at the hands of men and to hold onto the hope that God himself will raise us up. But for you there will be no resurrection to life."

**15** Next they brought the fifth and maltreated him.

**16** Looking at the king, he said: "You have authority over human beings, mortal as you are, and you do what you please. But do not think that God has abandoned our people.

**17** Keep watching, and you will see his great power, and how he will torment you and your descendants."

**18** After him they brought the sixth. When he was about to die, he said: "Do not deceive yourself to no purpose. We are suffering these things on our own account, because we have sinned against our own God, and things worthy of astonishment have befallen us.

**19** But do not suppose that you will go unpunished for having dared to fight against God."

**20** The mother was especially admirable and worthy of honorable memory. Although she watched her seven sons perish within a single day, she bore it with good courage because of her hope in the LORD.

**21** She encouraged each of them in the language of their fathers. Filled with a noble spirit, she reinforced her womanly feeling with a man's courage and said to them:

**22** "I do not know how you came to be in my womb. It was not I who gave you life and breath, nor I who arranged the elements within each of you.

**23** Therefore the Creator of the world, who shaped the first formation of humankind and devised the origin of all things, will in his mercy give life and breath back to you again — since you now hold your own lives cheap for the sake of his laws."

**24** Antiochus felt that he was being treated with contempt, and he was suspicious of the reproachful voice. Since the youngest was still alive, he not only appealed to him in words but promised on oath to make him rich and enviable if he would abandon his ancestral ways, and that he would take him as a Friend and entrust him with public office.

**25** Since the young man would not listen to him at all, the king summoned the mother and urged her to counsel the youth to save himself.

**26** After much urging on his part, she undertook to persuade her son.

**27** But leaning close to him, she spoke in their native tongue, mocking the cruel tyrant: "My son, have pity on me. I carried you nine months in my womb and nursed you for three years, and I have reared you and brought you to this point in your life and cared for you.

**28** I beg you, my child, to look at the heaven and the earth and see everything that is in them, and to recognize that God did not make them out of things that existed. And in the same way the human race came into being.

**29** Do not be afraid of this butcher, but prove worthy of your brothers. Accept death, so that in God's mercy I may receive you back again together with your brothers."

**30** While she was still speaking, the young man said: "What are you waiting for? I will not obey the king's command, but I obey the command of the law that was given to our fathers through Moses.

**31** But you, who have contrived all sorts of evil against the Hebrews, will certainly not escape the hands of God.

**32** For we are suffering on account of our own sins.

**33** And if our living LORD is angry for a little while, for the purpose of rebuke and discipline, he will again be reconciled with his own servants.

**34** But you, unholy wretch, most vile of all men — do not be lifted up in vain nor buoyed by hollow hopes, since you raise your hand against the servants of God.

**35** You have not yet escaped the judgment of the almighty, all-seeing God.

**36** For our brothers, after enduring a brief suffering, have drunk of ever-flowing life under God's covenant; but you, by the judgment of God, will receive just punishment for your arrogance.

**37** I, like my brothers, surrender body and soul for the laws of our fathers. I call upon God to show mercy soon to our nation, and through trials and plagues to make you confess that he alone is God,

**38** and through me and my brothers to bring to an end the wrath of the Almighty that has justly fallen on our whole nation."

**39** The king was enraged and handled him more savagely than the others, inflamed by the young man's contempt.

**40** So he too died undefiled, trusting completely in the LORD.

**41** Last of all, after her sons, the mother died.

**42** Let this be sufficient concerning the eating of sacrificial food and the extreme tortures.

---

## Translator's Notes

- **v. 6, Mosaic quotation**: The quotation is from Deuteronomy 32:36 (the Song of Moses). The citation in context of martyrdom is deliberate: Moses's song prophesied both judgment and compassion.
- **v. 9, "everlasting renewal of life"**: Greek *anabiōsin aiōnion* — literally "eternal coming-back-to-life." This is the clearest statement of bodily resurrection in pre-Christian Jewish literature, predating Paul's letters and the Gospel accounts of the resurrection. The second son asserts resurrection as certainty, not merely hope.
- **v. 11, "received these from Heaven... hope to receive them back"**: The third son's statement about his hands and tongue connects to the resurrection: the specific body parts used in fidelity will be restored. This particularized resurrection theology — not just "eternal life" but the specific body — is significant.
- **v. 14, "for you there will be no resurrection to life"**: The fourth son introduces the asymmetry: resurrection is for the faithful, not for the persecutors. This is a decisive theological claim — persecution does not end in equal eternal outcomes.
- **v. 21, "womanly feeling with a man's courage"**: This reflects ancient gender conventions (courage/virtue as masculine). The author inverts the expected — a woman performing the act of greatest *andreia* (manly courage). The mother is the most heroic figure in the chapter.
- **v. 28, creation ex nihilo**: "God did not make them out of things that existed" (*ouk ex ontōn epoiēsen auta ho theos*) is the earliest explicit statement of creation from nothing in extant Jewish or Christian literature. This verse became foundational for later theological discussions of divine omnipotence and creation.
- **vv. 37–38, intercessory martyrdom**: The seventh son explicitly frames his death as atoning — his suffering is intended to end the wrath on the nation. This concept, that the death of the righteous has vicarious value, became central to later Christian martyrdom theology and appears in Paul (Romans 3:25) and the Letter to the Hebrews.
- **v. 41, the mother's death**: The mother's death is recorded in a single clause, after all seven sons. The brevity is devastating. She outlived each of her children to encourage them; the narrator says nothing about her own end except that it came.
